Yeah, room 102 in the history building anyway, Tulane University. And this is Rio 1 of, let me give you a name too. No? Mm-hmm. Henry, come in. And my name is Dick Allen. Let's run it back and see how it recorded.
Say, uh.

I think we'll skip over your career as a musician if you don't mind for the time being. Not at all. And, uh, go on to, uh, your scholarly endeavors. What you think, uh, you've seen. I'll let you take over and discuss it and make my end of it as vague as possible.

Well, this will have to be very general. But, uh, anybody who wants to support the generalities, but particulars, will be able to find evidences here in the written material, at least some of the stuff I've done. Uh, one thing that I believe is easily proved is that New Orleans was a unique city in a very real sense. Different from any other American city, where the other American cities all much more like each other than any of them were like New Orleans. And I think this uniqueness, uh, as much as anything, caused jazz music to originate here, in spite of, uh, some of the current theories to the contrary. And, uh, one of the aspects of this uniqueness, uh, besides the racial mixtures, the, the cross, uh, mingling of so many different cultures, all of them bringing their music. Perhaps the easiest way they could communicate was through music at first. But one of the other and important, uh, differences was this tremendous desire for dancing here in this town. Uh, I've often thought that probably dancing grew here to be much more established as an amusement than anywhere else for probably two reasons. One was that this town was out of the way, and therefore, uh, not so easily, uh, able to get traveling, uh, entertainment, or, uh, things like that. And also not so easy for the people here to get to other towns, as for instance, the people in Philadelphia could visit New York and vice versa. And the other being that with so many different nationalities, with different languages so early here, the one kind, the one form of social amusement that they could all participate in, because no language was necessary, was dancing. But whatever the reason, dancing was a great overwhelming amusement and occupation here, with an enormous number of dance halls, both full-time and part-time. Now in the early years, the, uh, performers, teachers, the performers in the French opera, and other musicians like that, all engaged in playing for dance music. But so also did a lot of Negro bands in pre-Civil War days. But after the Civil War, uh, a certain, uh, reluctance on the part of the white professional music, uh, musicians to play, to play for dancing. And especially white men, it was considered a sort of, uh, inferior occupation for a white man to take up music. It was much better that he take up business. And, uh, uh, with the exception of the musicians in the French opera, very few white men participated in music as a livelihood. And those in the French opera were imported periodically from abroad. And yet the love for dancing carried over. And this meant that sort of by default, the trade of dance musician came more and more to be, uh, the province of the Negro, specialized in by the Negro, much as some other trades in this town, uh, such as masonry, fancy masonry, were a specialty of the Negro. And I think for this, that, that, that here is the main thing. The, uh, the Negro has the trade of playing for dancing. Dancing is extremely popular. And jazz, I think anybody would agree, was in its origins a functional music. It was a music played for dancing. Now, of course, uh, the, uh, outward forms that it would take, uh, this instrumentation, uh, in the brass, clarinet, trombone, and other brass horns, uh, was much influenced, as, again, I think is commonality, by the, uh, street marching bands that were modeled, uh, first after the French and, uh, then also after the German. As early as the 1930s, there were a number of German marching bands in the city attached to, uh, German militia. As early as what? The, the 1830s, I must say. Uh, and that is, that is European. But, again, this town was an especially crazy town for parades. Parades, uh, would, uh, be so frequent on a Sunday, spontaneous parades, that often the church couldn't get through its services if the day was nice and the doors were open. Because the bands would be, uh, out in the streets and parading around by eleven or even ten o'clock in the morning on Sundays. And this, too, goes into the stream of jazz, and I think it could be shown that while martial music was popular everywhere, nowhere in the United States were parades as popular as they were in New Orleans. Well, I see, Dick, uh, parades. Dancing. Dancing. And then the instrumentation of the French and German, uh, street bands would naturally have an influence. I should mention that in, even in pre-Civil War days, there were a great many Negro bands that paraded with, uh, militia companies or just spontaneously, as well as white bands. And, uh, there are even evidences, uh, uh, uh, in the, uh, pre-Civil War period of, uh, what today we would call a second line. Certainly great crowds often followed some of these bands, the Negro bands especially, laughing and shouting and dancing about in the streets, which implies that the music was at least, uh, lightened considerably from a ponderous kind of march. And all these things are, uh, distinctive and unique here. Uh, I think that any claim that jazz really started elsewhere, uh, is, uh, not too well supported. Now, it may be, of course, evolution of music being what it is, and jazz partaking to a great extent, uh, uh, of American characteristics and drawing in from American culture. Uh, it may well be that this music might have evolved more slowly in other places, and might have been evolving in other places, which is why I think that, uh, jazz was able to spread so rapidly. But the, uh, the birth of jazz in any recognizable form, uh, would have to, in my opinion, be placed in New Orleans.
Well, what about the rest of the country, as compared with New Orleans, as far as general musical sophistication is concerned? Both Negro and white, I'm talking about.

Well, it depends on the period you're talking about. In the, uh, pre-Civil War period, New Orleans is unmistakably miles ahead of the rest of the United States. It is a musical center in the United States. No question about that. And, uh, this was not exclusive with the whites. There were a great many Negro musicians who were taught by the white musicians playing in the French Opera, and in, uh, uh, the St. Charles Theater Orchestra, which was a very, very fine orchestra, uh, also. And these Negro musicians, in turn, were often employed as teachers for the children of, uh, white families. Quite a, quite a lot of musical, uh, interchange there. And, uh, either for these orchestras or for the opera, or for the general musical environment, no, no other city in pre-Civil War, United States came up to New Orleans. Even Boston. Even Boston. When the, uh, when the French Opera here went on tour, and it toured from 1827 to 1833, with the exception of one year, 1832, when the cholera epidemic was very strong in all the country, uh, north as well as south. And, uh, six of those seven years, the French Opera was on tour. They introduced, uh, uh, many things to Boston. They, they gave Boston, in fact, probably its, uh, first taste of opera like that. And they, they toured, not, not in every year did they hit all these cities, but in various years, they hit Boston, New York, Philadelphia, and Baltimore. And, uh, they did a great deal to revive all interest in opera in those cities. After all, the, many books will say that the first opera in the United States, uh, to amount to anything, uh, was the presentation by a Garcia troupe in New York City in 1825 of, uh, uh, Rossini's, uh, Barbara Seville. And that had played in its entirety here in 1823, two years earlier. And this company went on tour to New York in 27, just two years after the Garcia troupe. And the reviews uniformly appraised this as being a better ensemble, a better organized opera company. Uh, at a time when a lot of the instruments were either totally unknown or very little known in northern cities, this orchestra here, which was over 35 pieces or so, and had such instruments as bassoons and oboes, introduced these instruments in many of these cities. And when you come to, uh, post-Civil War, of course, you have the reconstruction problems, which hit New Orleans heavily up until 1876 or so. Uh, but the, uh, general interest in music and in parades, uh, was so persistent that it lasted well into the post-war period. Not long ago I heard a man visiting New Orleans, and he used a phrase, which is a rather good phrase for the city. He said that every time he came to New Orleans, and this is in the 1950s now, every time he came to New Orleans, he always found the city halfway between a ball and a parade. And I think it was always that way.
But they had academic music games, they mostly in the form of opera? That was the principal academic music, opera.

They, uh, had an amateur society before the Civil War called the Philharmonic Society that played, uh, attempted to play, uh, symphonic pieces. And the opera orchestra would play symphonic pieces. They gave a great many smaller concerts, which helped the opera musicians to pay their expenses and, uh, make a better salary. But the chief classical endeavor was far and away opera, no question about it. Mm-hmm. In fact, at one time in 1837, I believe it was, you could go out on a Friday night here and choose from among three operas. And then the same on Saturday night, choose from among three operas, which is remarkable in a city which was still fairly small by today's standards.
Mm-hmm. But, uh, well in 1837 Atlanta was nothing. Hardly on the map. Yeah. Uh, so you, you had so much like that. But Charleston was an old city and…

Yes, and has had some, uh, history and they had, of course, the St. Cecilia Society and Charleston and a choral history. Uh, but nothing like a permanent resident opera company. This was the only permanent resident opera company in the United States in those days. Mm-hmm. In fact, uh, you might say, uh, possibly the only, uh, really long-term continuous one until the, uh, advent of, uh, post-Civil War Chicago opera, Metropolitan Opera and San Francisco opera. This city was, uh, in this business from, well really almost from 1800 on. In fact, the first, uh, theater was opened in 1792 and there were operas performed in the 1790s. They couldn't have been, the production couldn't have been much, but they were trying and they were on the track. After 1819, then they had imported good-sized orchestras from mainly France, but Italy also and Germany. Uh, that is musicians from these countries making up the orchestra. Mm-hmm. All of them bringing with them a good deal of their own classical tradition and ways and approaches. But, of course, also pouring in here all the time down the Mississippi River was every bit of, uh, country and folk music that the United States had. Coming in with boatmen and all. And, uh, these boatmen, uh, for lack of other amusements, went to the opera. Really?
Oh, sure.

They, they'd fill the balconies and, uh, much to the annoyance of a lot of the, uh, study customers because they'd chop on apples and crack nuts and, uh, all sorts of things like that. You see, there were, after the St. Charles Theater opened, well, even earlier, uh, the first American theater to be built specifically for that purpose was opened in 1823 and that was a theater on Camp Street. Sometimes called the American theater, sometimes called the Camp Street Theater. And, uh, it used, uh, mounted operas. Now, it was never as good as the, uh, Orleans Theater, which was the French, uh, opera theater. But it did mount operas and, uh, some of them were successful. And, uh, even such a thing as, uh, the Freischutz, in the somewhat truncated version, was first played in New Orleans in the Camp Street Theater. But then, uh, in the 1830s, the St. Charles Theater, I think the first opening was 1835, and then there was a fire and it was rebuilt and opened again, but the St. Charles Street Theater, the St. Charles Theater was open. They had a huge orchestra, maybe, maybe 35 pieces or so, and were definitely out to rival the French, the Orleans Theater, where the French opera was. And to do this, they imported from Havana a very fine Italian opera troupe, a singing Italian opera. And, uh, in their first seasons, uh, uh, used, uh, represented such operas as, uh, Norma and, uh, uh, composers like, uh, along with Bellini, like, uh, well, Rossini had been played before, but they did more of Rossini. And, uh, the Italian opera as it existed at the time, so that you had the—what was called the French Opera—and even this is a misnomer— the French Opera House by no means confined itself to the French composed operas. operas. They used every opera there was, merely changing the lyrics to French, and thus Der Freischütz became Robin de Bois in the French theater.
What about the audience now? It wouldn't be all French, certainly.

No, it was, again, amusements were limited. However, after the American Theater opened, even the one on Camp Street and then later the St. Charles, there was a great tendency for the French to go to their side and the Americans to go to their side. But both theaters, this is true more often than the American Theater, tried to bring in attractions that would draw the patrons away from the other theater. Thus the American Theater would bring in French dancers, Celestine and Constance and things like that, hoping to draw the audience away from the French theater. But this only led to a great many Frenchmen to complain that they were denied the pleasure of seeing these dancers, since they didn't appear in the French theater. They considered they were denied the possibility and they would importune the management to get them over to their side so that they could go with propriety and see them. A good deal of rivalry that way. But always there were a great many English-speaking Americans or English-stock Americans who would contend French theater and vice versa.
What about Negroes? Did they have the free Negroes there or slaves?

Both. Both. They made a great many attempts to borrow the slave. But again, here's another thing that I guess you wouldn't find any place else in the United States, the whole state of a slave in a city like New Orleans. It's different and it's really not been studied yet. I've gotten only a sort of glimpse into it. But the outside of house servants, most the slaves here were skilled workers of one kind or another, and they worked for a wage. And the wage would be paid by anybody needing them, and their owner would then perhaps just take a monthly stipend from the slave. Say, if the slave earned 80 dollars a month, he might turn over 10 dollars a month to his owner. And it was on that basis that his owner might have invested in him. He might actually buy a slave knowing that he had a certain earning power. And his work more often than not necessitated that the slave live on his own, paying his own room and board. And that meant that his hours were free outside of his working hours. And since the city had so many free Negroes anyway, it was pretty hard to tell on the street who was a slave and who was a free Negro. And the free Negroes having their own dances for themselves, that is, I'm trying to distinguish those from the so-called quadrant balls or mixed dances, which were very abundant. The free Negroes would have dances and they couldn't tell whether there were slaves there or not. On one occasion, the police raided such a dance after a fight and they arrested 75 males. And when they registered them, it was found that 50 out of the 75 were in fact slaves all at this free Negro ball. And at the theaters, even though promises were made to the free Negroes who had a section in the balcony reserved for them, or in the French, in the Orleans area, a whole balcony reserved for them, the management promised often that they would make every effort to keep slaves up, that no slaves would come in. But again, how could you really tell? It's true that the slave was supposed to have a pass from his master to be on the streets like that, but the businessman at the door is not about to turn away a paying customer for lack of a pass. So if the slaves did get a chance to attend these operas and other musical functions, I don't know in what number, nobody will ever know that.
Well, would the free Negro have to carry any papers identifying in that side?

He had to have papers that would show that, or at least it would be advisable for him to have his papers of freedom on them all the time. However, New Orleans was not like a lot of the rest of the South, at least up until the 1850s, and I mean, did it even begin to crack down. It was a much more tolerant, lenient city. The Negroes of the city had a society of some sort that they called the Philharmonic Society prior to the Civil War, and I've even seen the tantalizing indications that possibly white musicians played in society with them on occasion, but I haven't been able to pin that down yet. There are hints to this effect. They had, for a brief time, they had their own theater, and they had their own theater, which they hoped to put on opera, and they did put on vaudeville, although apparently it wasn't a very long-term success. But they were always in the musical stream of New Orleans as much as anybody else was, Negro and Slate. What about, it just occurred to me,
Caldwell also was involved in promoting boxing, you know, the early theater, James Paul was. I wonder if they had any bands at boxing matches in it. Have you come across that?

I don't know. I haven't come across any such thing, and I've perused all the papers as closely as I can, but I'm not so sure, and I'm getting outside of anything I know much about, but I'm not so sure it was boxing. Very well known then, they might have had a boxer that they brought over or something like this, but Well they had them. I tend to think of boxing as post-Civil War.

Well I'll get in that class just spoke on the heavyweight championship and show if he was involved in some, I think a heavyweight championship match with an English rocker who he imported. I'll have to look it up.

He was a promoter all the way. He started the first Gasworks here, and he was in other business ventures, which went up and down, and the theater to him was another such venture, although I think his heart was always more in the theater. He'd started himself in an English company that he brought here in it was either 1817, I think it was 1817, and rented a little decrepit theater on St. Philip Street.

Well you hear about it later so much, playing between rounds is something I can't imagine happening today, but certainly within the memory of living people. I played between rounds. You played between rounds, right? Where?

In the military services. But that there of course is different. They had the bands, and the bands were always there to fight. Well there were a lot of occasions that were sporting where they had bands, and I just have never seen it in connection to boxing. But I don't know that you'd exactly call it a sport, but they were very fun in the fireworks exhibitions, and big blow-offs of fireworks, and you always have a band for these things in the country wherever they set up the firework exhibition. Or there might be a joint thing, a balloon ascension, and fireworks, and a band, always a band, and those things you can always find a band, a good musical monzique of some kind. It would be part of it, just an integral part of it. And then usually, the same band might turn to for dancing after the fireworks had gone off. It was very seldom that they had a band for any occasion, outside of a church service, that dancing didn't follow, and the band just converted to dancing. Of course they used the orchestras in the churches here, at least in the St. Louis Cathedral, and a custom that you don't see much of anymore, of playing for masses and playing for regular services. Sometimes as many as a 50-piece orchestra in the church.
What sort of racing did they have then? Horses and mules? Anything else?

I guess Dr. Hogan, I have to tell you more about that. I know there was a couple of clubs that got started very early here. One was called the Jockey Club or something like that, but I haven't followed. You haven't come across anything on bands? No, no, and in this respect, I can say I looked at it. You see, I looked at everything, but always looking for music, and if I didn't see music,
that was the end of my interest in it. What about the lake? Did they have music out

that much in those breaks over the water? Yes. There were hotels on the lake. In fact, the man that built the original, Arlie Sater, John Davis, had a hotel on the lake at one time, and they had music in those hotels for dancing, because hardly anything that didn't have dancing that connected with it existed. They even had dancing as far up here as Bay St. Louis, and ran special cruise boats from here for a weekend, you see, in Bay St. Louis, bringing the businessmen back to work in time for Monday morning after a hectic weekend of skating and dancing at Bay St. Louis. Would they run trains too? I've never seen trains going to the Bay St. Louis. No, trains were still, after all, pretty much in their infancy in the 1830s.
That's how far you've gotten now, you've returned to it. 1841. 1841. Well, I've gone through some,

quite a few, all the books, descriptive books and memoirs through to the Civil War, but the most fruitful mine is in the newspapers, and this is very tedious work. You've got to go through them column by column, and I've gotten there into the close of the opera season of 1840, 1841, midway through 1841. Slaves even had, and I like to mention this while I think of it, but slaves, you see, even had balls that were acknowledged to be slave balls. This was, this was, dances, this was common here, and the very evening of the Civil War, one diary of a New Orleans family records that, how they were, everyone was excited because their slaves were dialing up to go to a slave ball, and you get some insight into the social relations because some of the people they were going with were free Negro, but married to the slaves, and all in all it was probably about four or five in this particular diary, and they were going to a ball which was celebrating the secession of Louisiana, which certainly shows that music comes first. Oh yeah. And dancing. And of course, one thing you're almost sure of, of course this is an inference, but everything I've read and studied makes me feel that Negro musicians would commonly play for white dances. I don't mean to say that Negroes played most of the white dances, but all white musicians played in the pre-Civil War days for dancing, but this didn't bother the Negro. Great men Negro musicians also played, and sometimes one dance hall might have Negro music on some nights and white music on other nights, but I feel quite certain that white musicians did not play for slave balls or pre-Negro balls, you see, so this in itself gave the

Negro wider feel. Well that condition exists until today, I mean really, the Negro bands play for both races, the white bands don't play for white. Yes. Well that brings up the point with me now, at what period did you say it became more fashionable for a man to go into business, a white band to go into business? Well there was some feeling about this all the way through,

you see, in the early, oh in the 1820s and the 1830s and 40s, families tended to discourage a man who thought of taking up the piano or something, although they would have a genius like Gottschall, of course he left New Orleans when he was 10 or 11 years old to study for all the next years in France, the 1860s until he came back. But very few white men in New Orleans aspire to become, say, a performer in the orchestra of the French theater. But what happened to keep a lot of white musicians around and even growing in number, was a kind of reverse process. Every three or four years there had to be a heavy infusion of new blood into the French orchestra. For two reasons, either some who had been here two or three years wanted to return to Germany, or to France, to wherever they were from, Italy. And others liked it here and it drifted into other ways of making a living. Most often musicals are closely associated with it. For instance, they might become choir masters, they might become private teachers, they might get involved in promoting the dance halls, or there were myriad ways that they could sort of drift out of the opera, but remain here, adopt the city, and they were always enthusiastic musicians. They made a widening musical circle, and this thing continued through all those years. About every two or three years, either a complete new orchestra or at least a whole lot of new musicians came from abroad.

This is Reel 2, Henry Command, February 13th, 1963. We were talking there about the white musicians and how you had their replacements at the French opera. And what I was really getting at was in the early jazz days, and I don't know how much we know about that, but judging from the memories of people like Jack Lang, which is maybe even pre-jazz as we know it.
What does he go back to, Dick, about the 1890s?

No, before that. You see, he got his drums when they broke down the Cotton Exposition. He got his first real set of drums, but he had kids that he would play on toy instruments before that. He was born in 1873. So the thing that interested me and the early white bands that I hear about, I wonder what kind of social class they came from. Musicians, you're talking

about playing at the opera, would they be accepted? Yes, they were even very much respected, the musicians in the opera. Now, social class... You see, there wasn't such a strong distinction between the classical musicians. The musician who played in the French opera also played for dancing. Sometimes the whole French opera orchestra played for a really fine, fine gala dance. But more often, they went out as leaders of very smaller groups in all of these dance halls. One time there were always an enormous number of dance halls. And it added a kind of to build their dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear what they called vaudeville, which might be a whole lot lighter. And even when they played opera, they mixed it with other entertainment. Between the acts there might be sword swallowing or tightrope walking or dancing. They called it rope dancing. They had duels. They had acrobats. They had demonstrations of all kinds. They just mixed the entertainment in together. There wasn't very much of a divorce along class lines of high class and low class. Now, among the dances, there were, of course, all kinds of classes there. And some people, and a great many people, in an endeavor to keep their dances less public and more refined, had strictly private subscription dances where everyone had to sign up for ten or twelve balls in advance for season. They'd know the finances were there that way. And they'd have a series of ten or twelve subscription balls, as they called them. And you can find a class level in advances every step of the way, down to what were really brawls, mixed color, whites and negroes of both sexes all mixing it together in what must have been a pretty wild night. After the war, there I don't have first-hand research. I can't say any more broadly than you can there. That's one of the things that I hope to get to. And it's a good question to raise for that period. It needs to be answered to find out what the social status of a musician was actually here, after the war. In some ways, one would think that maybe he had a better position than the musician in many other American cities. Certainly, we know the negro musicians were idolized, if we can believe, these accounts by their own people. They say that Bolden was such a great hero. And the military band tradition was certainly very, very strong here. And don't forget that after the war, in the United States as a whole, you began to get the emergence of the Symphony Orchestra, and this carried with it a good deal of respect. You had these great military bands, like the one from Boston, I forget his name, Pat, it's an Irish name. Gilmore. And that band played here, by the way, in New Orleans, at the time when he had all those cannon wired up to shoot off together in the overture of 1812 and everything, something like a hundred cannon wired up to go off together. And they had a huge band here. So it's not very long before you begin to get the, well, Seuss's band and the American band in general. By the 1890s, you're in full swing with band concerts in the park. And like, so I don't know, I don't know.

I can imagine that the status of a musician didn't drop too far. But still, it wasn't so much frowning upon it socially. I wouldn't want to leave that impression. When the white male of a New Orleans family didn't learn music, I think it was just simply that this wasn't a good enough perfection financially. There was more money to be made in a whole lot of other things than there was to be made in music as a career.
Well, uh,

It seems to me that until the twenties, around in there, the professional jazz musician in New Orleans came definitely from a working class family. And he didn't, uh, maybe have all the advantages of a musical education. I don't know.

I think this fits in though, you see? Just as a, look at it this way. A great many Negroes today, Uh huh. Excel in music, just as they excel in, say, football. Because this is one of the avenues that is open to them, where they can make a mark and go a considerable distance. And this might attract a larger percentage. Let's say that among the whites, there might be a larger percentage having a good deal of native musical ability. But they have opportunities that are so good in the field of law or business or something else. That they channel into that. Now, this was, uh, as I tried to, uh, indicate, I think that before the Civil War, as the war approached, the very profession of, uh, of, uh, playing for dancing came to be, uh, more and more Negro. And then after the Civil War, uh, it got to be almost, uh, a Negro specialty. And due to this, of course, I imagine it would even attract more Negroes in it. He would just go into it as a, as a matter of course. And then White just didn't go into it because he had better opportunities than something else. It wasn't so much just a case of looking down the nose at a musician. When Gottschalk came here in the 1850s, of course, he was a hometown boy, but nevertheless, musicians were idolized that came here. If they were good musicians, they were idolized. When, when Johnny Lynn came here, uh, it was pandemonium. And Barnum actually had to, uh, put a fake Johnny Lynn off the boat in order to draw the crowd away while he got the real Johnny Lynn into her apartment in the Pantavo building. Uh, of course, this was an outstanding attraction, but all visiting musicians were according respect. Mm-hmm. It's just that while you might respect the trade and everything, you wouldn't want your own boy to do it when he could make twice or three times the money in something else or possibly inherit a family business. So just gradually, sort of by default, uh, the, uh, business of providing music for dancing came to, uh, be more and more, especially of the Negro era. But I don't mean to imply that there ever was a time when there weren't white bands and white dance bands.
What about funeral music in those days? Can you infer anything about it? You come across that?

Well, uh, pre-Civil War days I'm talking about. Pre-Civil War days. The, the, uh, the beginning, sort of, with the great love they had for military funerals here and all that. You see, they had all these veterans of the battle of, uh, January 15th, and there were, uh, uh, 1815, January 8th, 1815, the, the battle of New Orleans. And, uh, uh, uh, uh, even before that battle there was a great, uh, militia tradition here. And almost everyone was organized into this, that, or the other militia company, which loved to have a different uniform, get out and parade, and, uh, had its band usually attached to it. And the militia company wasn't much good without, uh, its own band for parade. In addition, the Masons were very, uh, strong here. And, uh, other French, uh, uh, societies, uh, springing out of the French Revolution, were present here. And then with the advent of, uh, Germans and Irish and other groups, Spanish, they tended to form national groups, usually modeled into something either semi-militia, semi-fraternal, or fully fraternal and semi-military, something like this, uh, Masonic. And, uh, so that by the 1820s, uh, most, uh, most anybody would be able to have a military funeral, because somewhere along that line he belonged to a veterans organization or a fraternal organization or something. And there were a great, great many military funerals, some very long and some, uh, short. And I think this, uh, uh, was, uh, taken over by the Negro, who simply modeled himself after these things. Uh, probably more military funerals here in New Orleans than anywhere else. And if they couldn't get ahold of a body, they still didn't stop from having a military funeral. They had one for Napoleon, and, uh, I believe, I remember, that they had one for Lafayette, too. It's just, uh, a thing to do. And sometimes, uh, uh, more than one ban in these things. Now, you find in the, uh, curious note in the, uh, they had a series of yellow fever epidemics in the 1850s, 1857, a very bad one. And you find, uh, here that plenty of people were being, uh, buried, you see. And a lot of them were buried with these military parades. And you find complaints against these parades on two grounds. One was that there were so many of them, and they made so much noise, they were disturbing the people who were critically ill. But the other one, and this is the really significant one to me, is the fact that editors and reporters, uh, and moralists, complained that these bands, when they came back from the grave, played, and they, these are the exact words, unseemly music. Now, whether that just simply meant that they went off into a rousing good march song coming back, uh, or whether it meant that the music was even, uh, uh, possibly just a hint of a, uh, of a jazzed-up march. After all, all you have to do to, uh, any march that's a melodic march is kind of hit the, hit the off-beats a little harder than usual, and you get a, uh, a jazzed-up feeling to it. It doesn't have to be ad lib. It's like a rag very much.
Uh-huh. It's rocked and everything.

And, uh, whatever it was, it was unseemly music coming back from the graves. And, of course, you can see how many of these things there were when they had to complain that the noise was continually disturbing the, the patients in the hospitals. That never died out either. And I suppose as the Negroes took over, uh, these customs and, uh, it became the thing to do, of course, uh, you know, today, and especially more so twenty or thirty years ago, uh, many Negroes aspired to belong to one or another, uh, burial or fraternal, uh, organizations to ensure a good, solid funeral, which usually meant possibly a band and a parade.

Uh, I know there are a lot of things we haven't covered along that line, but I did want to get a little bit about, uh, your life down. It's, uh, it's a matter of record how much research you've done here, maybe a dissertation, copy of it over there. But, uh, first thing I'd like to ask anybody is when they were born and where, if you don't mind.

I was born in, uh, 1915, November 3rd, in upstate New York, Saratoga Springs, New York. And, uh, that was a city which was a summer resort for many, many years. Uh, in fact, uh, pre-Civil War days, it was one of the common resorts of, uh, wealthy New Orleanians, uh, to go to Saratoga. And Edna Ferber's novel, Saratoga Trump, you know, it's a lane between New Orleans and Saratoga Springs. But, when I was of, uh, an age to notice anything, say, in the early 1920s, Saratoga was a town that, in the summertime, had an enormous number of bands. Uh, perhaps all the best bands that were around in the country, uh, played at Saratoga in those summers, uh, four, five, six, seven, or eight at a time. They had that many big nightclubs, actually, they were gambling houses. And, uh, for example, uh, Early Lopez, Paul Whiteman, Ben Pollack, when he had a band, and any number of others that would come to your mind were there, and any kid could go around from place to place if he were minded to, and just hang around outside and listen all night long to these bands.
Which Lopez was that?
Vincent Lopez. Uh, he's still going, you know. He ought to write a book, that guy, because he's been around an awful lot of music for an awful long time. Vincent Lopez.
I had some early jazz musicians, when I forget who there were, too.

I had some, there weren't, in the early 1920s, there weren't so many big bands, but what all of them would have some jazz musicians. I wouldn't imagine that if Whiteman had come along in the 30s, say, especially after 35, and everyone's age was at the same time, and I don't think Whiteman would have had a chance to have T. Garden or Biderbecke or any of these guys. They would have more likely have been with bands that were swinging more, playing more, you see. But in those days, this kind of hotel band was the dominant band, and there weren't as many of them. Radio multiplied them. Once radio really took hold, it multiplied them radio and records. But in the early 1920s, the really big names, you could pretty well know most of them. In the 30s you couldn't. It would take you all day to recite the number of bands there were. You just wouldn't remember all of them.
So what you had then was a lot of bands with local reputations, territory bands I guess they called them.

Oh, far from territory. You mean generally? Before the 30s. Well, the bands I mentioned, like Lopez and Whiteman, of course, were nationally known. Yeah. They were the, Saratoga got the best that could be gotten. It was very wealthy. And it's one month, actually for one month, the month of August, when the racing season was on. Maybe a five week season or so. Sometimes it was. But there were territory bands, of course. New England was loaded with a number of them. And the New York. Western New York, Pennsylvania, and Jersey area was loaded with a number of them. Some of them were bands that later became big name bands in the 30s. They were embryonic. They were on their way. Sometimes there were bands put together for summer barnstorming, college kids and the like. And a lot of them went on to… I remember one band that came in from New England named Don Gann. If I remember correctly, Gann or Gann. Most of which later became the Les Brown band. The early Les Brown band.
Yet he came out of Duke, didn't he?
I know it. I've never reconciled that. But somebody that really dug into newspapers in those days, or whatever other sources there were, could maybe unravel things like that.
Well, those personnel were subject to change, I'm very reckoning.

Yes, and whether Les Brown had joined this Don Gann band, or whether he just took it over, or whether he may have been an arranger for it. Quite often the kind of story that you heard about how a band originated was romanticized, you know. And it'd give you the impression that this band had stuck together and fought its way up writers and movies and things like to depict things that way. That was hardly ever true. Very seldom did it happen. Usually as the band moved up, the personnel changed. Got better.
Well yeah, and Alito, his band broke up, he might just take up another man's band entirely.
Or higher, and anyway, temperaments being what they were, very few musicians could stand anybody very long in there. Always splitting up, moving up, moving around.
But did you play any musical instrument when you were growing up in Saratoga?
I started playing piano very early. I don't remember when. I didn't play it very well, but I played saxophone I guess from the time I was about twelve or so. I should make it 1927 or so. Late 1920s.
Did you play piano by ear?
No, I took lessons. Used to. Like a lot of kids. Did just about as well as a lot of kids.
I guess you hated taking lessons. I think.
Yes, indeed. Worse, I hated practicing.
And what inspired you to take up saxophone?

I always liked the pictures of saxophones in magazines. By this time you could hear a lot of it on the radio. I don't know who can explain these things, but I always had an affinity for the sound. I just really liked the sound of a sax or saxophones. There was an analogy too, isn't it? Yes, but it also sounded to me like much more than a novelty. I just liked the sound. I always had, so do. A good sax choir is one of my principal joys. And a fellow who was living in my house, he used to go off in periodic toots, the kind of genteel drunkards that you don't find much anymore in the country, sober for six months and then disappear for a week and come back. Boarder at the house, he came back after one of these toots with a saxophone and that was it. Where he got it, nobody knows, including him. What kind of saxophone? It was a buffet C melody. That was convenient because there were more C melodies around. You remember Trombauer played a C melody and Jack Purvis, who I believe possibly was from New Orleans, also played a C melody sax. It got a distinctive and very pretty sound on it. Jack who? Purvis. Oh, Pettis, huh?
Pettis, Pettis, yes.
Purvis is a trumpet player. No, Pettis, Jack Pettis.
Well, Pettis I think is from around Bungalusa. No, you're quite right.

Jack Pettis, definitely Jack Pettis. I heard his orchestra many times. He played up in Albany, New York, you know, visiting there, but that was close to my home and we could always hear the bands from Albany on the radio. You could read sheet music. You could read sheet music. This is what a lot of people did in those days. Got a whole piece of sheet music and got a whole piano player of some kind, drummer of some kind. And the C horn, you could read over your shoulder the melody line when you were in business.
No transposing, no problems. No transposing, no problems.

No transposing, no problems. That's right. And that's the way I started and apparently there was enough to be and I guess looking back, enough dances and so forth that a lot of people were willing to put up with some pretty sad music just in order to have some music. You had a good chance to pick up experience.
Did you take lessons on the same melody track?

I never took lessons on the saxophone, the clarinet. I sometimes was afraid to take lessons. I didn't want to mess around trying to change my way of playing. As long as I was getting along, alright. Well, actually you learn an awful lot from the college you worked with. A kid in those days, I don't guess that this is ever, it's certainly not possible anymore, it may never be possible again in America, but you could go, you could draw a thirty mile radius, a thirty miles, a circle, a thirty mile radius around my town, and I dare say you could find a hundred bands, big and small. And all of them, there was a great deal of sitting in and everything, or just listening. Both were instructive, sitting in and listening. As far as my age, I had the same enthusiasm for music, and there were many, made a point of this. Never missed a band, never missed going wherever there was a band, or wherever you could sit in. And this is from the age of twelve? No, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, after you got a little, you had to have some competence. You had to, you can't just sit in and blow nothing. You can't sit in and blow something. But you learn an awful lot sitting in. And then of course up there, being no colored bars, I often wonder how much this just had to do with perhaps shifting the scene of vitality in jazz from New Orleans to Northern cities. And the fact that you could sit in, now I'm not saying that in those early days you had mixed bands playing, you understand, as an organized professional group. That wasn't done. But there was plenty of sitting in. No bars there at all. And if a dance hall had a Negro orchestra, all the white musicians in the world could come there and sit in and play with them. That created no problem at all. So that you got an interchange there. And the Negroes were very instructive about jazz as they were playing it. They didn't try to sit on any secrets, at least the ones I knew. They were glad to show you everything that they could show you. You can't just transfer the way you play, but you can show a person a lot of tricks. So we had an environment that was wonderfully instructive. And then when you started playing, as you played with better bands, there were musicians drifting into that area from New York and from Canada and from Boston and from all around. Sometimes musicians already there were musicians. I remember when I was fourteen or fifteen or sixteen, there were musicians that were in their forties and had been playing quite a long time. I remember one especially when I came down from Canada. And he played up there for a while with Jack Denny when Denny was still starting up in Montreal. But he had a health problem and come to this area for his health, but still played occasionally. And playing with musicians like that, you learn a lot just playing with them. Jack Denny, huh? Yeah, Jack Denny was one of the bands that got nationally popular through radio. He used to have a program from CKAC, Montreal, I can remember very well. And had no brass band at all, just saxes and accordion. Later when he came down and made it bigger in New York he added brass, but he was popular for quite a while, Jack Denny. As I remember one time he had a Whitman Sampler album.
That's funny, I don't remember anything about him at all.

Well, we've talked about this at other times, Nick, and it really doesn't belong here, but somebody, someday, ought to dig into the big bands in America too. That whole era of bands before it's lost completely. You remember I often mention to you my favorite band up there, the Lonely Acres Band, and young Chinese Paul Tremaine and his Lonely Acres Band. I've never seen reference one to that any place. And I remember that band so well coming on the radio at noontime when I was a kid still in school, and playing tunes like Hand Me Down My Walking Cane and everything, big band swing style. And he did spirituals too, didn't he, Tremaine? Well, yeah, what was it called? Well, they'd do things like semi-spirrors, you know, gold and slippers, and maybe swing low sweet cherry, things like that.

Swinging them all. Did you ever know a fellow named Teddy Brewer, he later called himself Teddy Martin, he played Albert System clarinet on Bourbon Street, a non-human about 1950, I forget what happened to him. Fudd was playing piano with him some it seems to me, and a guy who played valve trombone, he told me something about Paul Tremaine.
Well, I'd like to meet him then, because that's the only other guy I've ever heard of that heard of Paul Tremaine, and yet I can tell you that band was...
Yeah, I've heard of him. Paul Barber and then he were talking about what that, I just remember. About Paul Tremaine's band? About Tremaine's band. Then I'd like to ask Barber about it.

Yeah, well I remember that was a very popular band. I know they were in Young's Chinese American restaurant in New York for years, and they must have come previously from someplace called Only Acres, maybe a dance hall or something, you know, they did that off, like the Casa Loma Band came out of a Casa Loma restaurant. And I understood later on that the guys were working there for about seventeen dollars a week and found a room and board, which was not uncommon for bands in those days, you used to work for very very little. Twelve, fifteen dollars a week and a room and board. And I don't know what ever became of that band. But I remember this, that at a time when the outstanding swing band, this is in the pre-swing era, if you could even call it that, a swing band, but jazz band or a big jazz band, as far as the public was concerned, was the Casa Loma Band. When you'd hear Tremaine, you'd recognize already that this was in advance in the loose, relaxed swing it had, much more like the later swing bands.
I didn't have that impression of it. I thought it was much more rikki-tikki and stiff in its rhythm, but it wasn't.

Well, again, not having records so that you can go back. Yeah. You know, I've heard recently some Goodman records that I remember distinctly, and this is later, in 1937, 38, I thought were great swinging things. And I hear them now and they sound pretty heavy and sodden with rhythm. So you never know what your impressions are like, but I remember this impression about the Tremaine band distinctly, that for its time, it seemed to me like an advance group that the loose swing had.
I have to find some records about them. I guess I will. I think I may have one at one time or another, but I may have had one.

I was hearing at the same time Don Redmond and bands like that, Jimmy Lunsford. Not very often though, you see, because the radio didn't play at Jimmy Lunsford or Don Redmond as often as you could get a band like Paul Tremaine, except because of the hotel situation.
Did you have any ideal saxophone player that you felt influenced your style earlier? Who did people look up to in those times?

It was the earliest I can remember when people looked up to Coleman Hawkins. That early, huh? Yes, sir. When he was playing with Fletcher Henderson. And I mean real early, I'd say, when he was playing with Fletcher Henderson. So many of the American musicians started to date Coleman from the time he came back from abroad and made that body and soul that he was playing Greyhorns way before then. One time I remember a guy called Mad Tale. My dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
This is Rio 3, Henry Comin, February the 13th, 1963. We're talking about Saxe Mansfield. He was one you liked.

Yeah, I don't think I would like him today, but he played in the Eysom Jones band. These are all pre-swing bands, but there were a lot of bands that played big band jazz. That didn't come out with the swing era, nor you know it's often said that that problem was solved with Fletcher Henderson when he began to write the line. He may have perfected it, but there were a lot of bands groping your way toward trying to play some kind of big band jazz or swing music before. And many bands that might be primarily so-called sweet bands, usually at any dance, you played in sets, and it was pretty often that you're trying to get a slow number and a medium number, say, and possibly now and again a waltz. Not much Latin then. But you always ended the set with an up-tempo, and it had to swing in some way. After all, the Castle Oma band was trying to grope toward this, and before that it was the Gene Goldkamp band, the Castle Oma band.
Yeah, well, of course, if the people knew him beforehand, it never started arranging. That's what I believe, yes. Yeah, well, Don Redman was doing his arrangements for him before that.
But, uh, oh, and I don't know. Then there was a guy in the Castle Oma band, I think his name was Pat Sullivan? No, Pat… The Tenor Club?
Yeah.

Pat Davis. Pat Davis. Pat Davis. He was much admired by almost all the saxophone players I knew. In fact, some of them, at one time he used a baritone mouthpiece on a tenor to get a broader sound, and that became a thing a lot of guys did, put a baritone mouthpiece on a tenor. But very soon they came to regard him as nothing. He wasn't really a lasting man or a lasting influence. Whereas Hutchins Ryder, a clarinet player, was good then and has been good all the way, and sounds remarkably good today.

Well, specifically, getting back to what I'm supposed to be researching, I want to get some of your attitudes about early New Orleans musicians that you've heard and have some sort of impression of. You know, whether they were considered corny or good, and how you knew them and why, and just anything.

Well, at the time that I broke into the business in a professional way, generally the New Orleans musicians were, or the New Orleans style was passe. This is a time when I was kept alive by some guys who were devoted to it, you know, more or less underground. But the average working musician, at least around my area, which would be New York area, regarded that whole kind of music as corny. They called it corny. Of course, they thought of themselves as being the utmost in modernity and so forth. But then when I went to New York, the revival, perhaps the first revival, was just beginning, and this revival really coincided, or even owed in part to Goodman's success. No doubt about that. And you remember, for a brief period, they got together as much of the original Dixieland Jazz Band as they could. And at that time, I met Larry Shields. I met him through New Orleans musicians that I had met and worked with. I met him specifically. I used to see Larry Shields and meet him up in an apartment in the Landseer Apartments in New York that was either, I know Sharky lived in that apartment, and Johnny Beresdorfer was living in that apartment.
So you met the Musicians' Ball, incidentally.
Oh, did you?
Well, the other musicians from New Orleans, it was kind of a convenient hangout, and Sharky

used to cook for us occasionally, Creole. And that's where I met Shields, and then in the same group of musicians, but in another place I met quite frequently Tony Parenti. And again, at the time he was considered pretty bad, pretty corny. In fact, I jammed with him in the apartment, and that was my impression of him. But he's still going pretty strong right now, as you know. And I thought of him as an old man then. When did you move to New York? It would be 1934, even 1933 possibly, as soon as I got out of high school. Well, Goodman wasn't a big man then. No. No. I remember very well the first Goodman broadcast on the National Biscuit Company deal that they had there, and the impact that that had on musicians around me. And I remember the first Goodman record that had any real wide circulation, both upstate, because I was New York City and my home were just a few hours apart, was a record of Sometimes I'm Happy, in which Arthur Rolini played a tenor solo and Berrigan was in the band. And the King Porter Stomp at the same time. These were the two records that really made the first big impression.
And George Van Epps and the Guitar Tealers was another big thing in that record to me.
If I'm not mistaken, he still had Frank Troll I think, didn't he?
He might have. I know Charlotte was Frank.

I see, to give you an example, in my hometown, the first time we heard Goodman was at a dance in my hometown, playing for Skidmore College. It just had been booked up there. And all the local musicians were around behind the bandstand. Krupa was with him then, and Frank Frobot, I distinctly remember that that night, Helen Ward. Arthur Rolini was playing tenor sax with him then. I also met Adrian Rolini in those days. I guess some people mentioned it somewhere, but it bears repeating. Adrian was primarily a saxophone player then. He hadn't gone into that trio deal yet. And he made for himself a little reed instrument that he bought the size of a good-sized fountain pen. He had a clip for it, even. He carried it in his pocket, and wherever he went, he felt like sitting in. He could pull this thing out of his pocket like a fountain pen, and by George, sit in and play on it.
That must have been easier to carry than anybody said. You see why he did that.
And it couldn't be more extreme from the saxophone. It was a remarkable thing.
It was an arrangement for Dixen Land Church. But… Were Shields playing then when you first met him? Yes.

He was playing with the revival of Dixen Land… Mm-hm… …the original Dixen Land Group. In fact, they had just finished at the Paramount Theater or something on stage… …very much playing. He was white-haired then… Mm-hm… But young in face and body, and certainly playing very well. And I will say this, I've never met anybody, any time, any place that didn't respect his clarinet play. At any period, you know, his styles changed. Whether they heard him in person or whether they heard records in their records, no matter what period they came from, they all acknowledged him to be a very great clarinet player. He must have had tremendous influence on a lot of people there as shields.

They had all those different fives, the Memphis Five and the Indiana Five and all, when the Dixieland Band made its impact early in the year. They all seemed to try to play like shields, model themselves on the Dixieland.
Must have been a major influence on the music.
Oh yeah.
This is not true of everybody else in the original Dixieland Band.
No, I think that, well I think that people look up to him, musicians and fans, more than any other man in that band.

I'm quite sure of that. But I remember when I went to New York, Miff Mole was around, and much respected already, and then there was a guy that they called Little Miff. I can't recall now who he was, but there was another Tramone player that they used to call Little Miff Mole. Little Miff at least.

Who are some of the people from that era who you think have been, I'm getting off of New Orleans again, which I wanted to stick with, but while we're at it, who are some of the people who have kind of forgotten, we talked about Hutch and Ryder before we ever had the tape machine on, as being one of the ones who's kind of forgotten.

Well a lot of them I guess are so forgotten that I can't even remember their names, but you used to hear, I can say this, there were in my town again in this racing season that brought all these big bands, there were also innumerable little nightclubs, there was a Negro Quarter in the town, and this Negro Quarter had many places that had anywhere from five to seven piece Negro bands, there might have been as many as eight or ten of these. And I don't think I ever went in any one of them and didn't hear guys that blew what I thought was just absolutely great horn, you know, and the nature of things, a lot of them never did make. The United States itself must be full of thousands of fine, unsung musicians that play a lot. But one thing about New Orleans, and I might forget, when I went to New York, a man that had just come there, or at least a man that had just come there, was Sharkey. And after a kind of slow start, as everybody does, between the six month union law and one thing or another getting known, Sharkey took a band into the old Knicks. I used to go down there often and sit in with the band. I sat in on tenor sax, no place really in the regular organization, but they didn't mind my sitting in. But he had practically an old New Orleans band there. He had Bill Bourgeois on clarinet, and Johnny Castang on drums, and George Brunis on trombone. And the bass player was Turk somebody or other who wasn't from New Orleans, and I've forgotten the piano player's name. At one time he had an English piano player I remember. He may be able to place him because he played around a lot subsequently with the guitar player, Eddie Conn, and that general group up there. But that band really made Knicks. It packed them in every night. This was a Dixieland craze for real then. And the place prospered so, and as you know they began to build a newer and bigger and better place across the street down a little bit. And when they did, Sharkey had every reason to think, I guess, that he would be the band there, the house band. And he did indeed open it, but he opened it with another band, Bobby Hackett, who also had his trombone player, George Brunis. Some things were done that Sharkey didn't know about, and before long he was out there. I think he had as much to do with building it as anybody did.
And Bobby got his trombone player.
Yes. Yes.
Was he playing louder than Hackett or? No. Brunis toned down or what?

No. For Bobby to be heard, Brunis would have had to tone down, because Bobby didn't play louder for the simple reason that he couldn't play louder. I later, but not too much later, played with Bobby myself. Played in his bands, both big and little. Played at the New York World's Fair with him, for example, with a little band. And played in a place on 52nd Street called The Troc, which is not there any longer, across from the second famous door, the more famous famous door, with a big band. And Bobby just never could play loud. He didn't have to look for it. You know, he never was an accomplished trumpet player as a trumpet player. The way I heard is, he was just a guy with a lot of fine ideas for trumpet. Not all of which he always was able to execute. But even his muffs were often pretty. Yeah.
Fantastic music.
Well he played guitar, you know, and I helped him a lot with getting unusual progressions. But even without that he had a beautiful ear.
Well did you play at Dick's? There's a regular number? No, no, no.
But I played there often. Often sat in?
Yeah, very often. Was it common for people to sit in there?

Well, no, but you see I had known all these guys so well, and the horn I played didn't get in anybody's way. To throw a tenor in with a Dixie group like that didn't hurt anything. I took pains that it didn't. And it meant that I got a chance to blow choruses with them, and I did blow a lot of them. It was a good way to practice and also to get yourself known by other musicians, because there were a lot of musicians that hung around. You almost had to do that sort of to break in in New York and get around and play whatever way you could. And I followed coming from the country to New York City. This was the one sure way. You get your horn out and get in and play. I played in places like Adrian's Tap Room always sitting in, you see. And Nixon, plenty of other places.
Who was at Adrian's Tap Room then?

There was a little four piece group. One thing I remember, Willie Lyon Smith was playing there on the single piano. And this little four piece group had a bass and a tenor sax. And Adrian would often play vibes with it, but he was also busy managing. He wasn't always on the bandstand. And I believe the piano, probably drums. And the tenor sax who was working there at the time I used to sit in was Artie Drillinger, D-R-I-L-L, Drillinger. And he's still around. He's somewhere, I think he's up in the studios now. He's still playing. He blew with a lot of good bands.
And he was a hot man there though.

Yes, well almost everybody in that period that came in was a hot man. But a lot of guys found out they weren't hot enough and then they became more legit or something. For instance, I had a fellow that came to New York with me and I had room for a while. He was from Cortland, New York, which is near Syracuse. And he played so hot in the Casco Mountains that we called it the nearest thing to a torrent or trumpet that we'd ever heard. And he still played a lot of jazz, but he made his biggest mark playing in bands like the Barnett Band and the Bob Crosby Band as the high trumpet man. Because when he played with Crosby for instance, Yank Lawson was also playing. Yank just played a little bit better jazz. And my friend is Lyman Bunk, his name was, he did have a tremendous lip, so he played the high trumpet parts. And this happened to many people that developed into lead men and developed into good double men playing many instruments, multiple instruments. They all could play some jazz, but just some of the fellows were specialists in it because they were better jazz men.

Did you know Elma and Nicholas, a clarinet player? Danny Gawka, a guitar player? They used to be around the taproom. At least they made some records with Rolini during that period. Well, there were two things that happened here.

First of all, there were so many musicians that you met. That union floor and the street around the union floor after union hours was just loaded with musicians and you don't remember, you know, you just didn't get their name or associate with them. And then the other thing that operates is the fact that I've forgotten a lot of the fellows' names. I've tried to recall in my own mind sometimes, many of the people that I work with, I can remember their face and the fact that I'm working with them better than I can remember their name. And in some cases I know I never will remember the name unless it's brought to my attention. I don't know.
Well, what about, say, Tony Almarico, was he up there for them? That period I'm trying to remember, or did you know him?
I guess he made trips up there, but I've only read this from later. I didn't meet him up there or know of him up there.
What about Fazzola? Did you know him?

Oh yes, everybody's in Fazzola. Just everybody. Fazzola came on the scene with the Bob Crosby band shortly after Goodman had generated all this interest in clarinet, and it was just a solid rave all the way, Fazzola's clarinet playing. And there again you have an example, because prior to that time, well, Eddie Miller played some clarinet, made one notable recording instead of fashion of clarinet, and then wasn't it Matty Matlock that played clarinet with that band too? Yeah. I remember when Fazzola came in, he was the king in that band.
What was the Miller record? Do you remember? It might sometime, Dick.

There was one low register clarinet thing that's become almost a standard, sort of like Bix's chorus on Birth and the Blues, one of these things that's a set of pattern. And much to my surprise upon it was Eddie Miller that had recorded that. It's in one of the standard big band, Dixieland numbers, like Muscat Ramble or Rampage Street, some of that, that's lots of numbers. And Miller, once we played that low, Newman clarinet chorus on it. Right in that shallow, move range of the clarinet, and big sonorous tone down there, and never getting up into the upper range.
Yeah, and that was kind of out of fashion then, wasn't it?

Well, it became a kind of characteristic of Dixieland. Often you see when they come to the trio and the Dixieland number that followed that form, the first clarinet chorus in that trio would be down in that register. And then the second one would move up more into the upper register.
But I don't associate low register with shallow, good, and the northern clarinet chorus. Oh no, no, no, no, that's right.
That was a distinction, Dixieland kind of thing. Usually came in on the trio movement, one of these march type things.
Did you play much with Foss in bands with him? Never played with him, no, no, never.
Never did.
You heard him with him? Plenty. With what, with big bands?
The Cosby band, maybe.

Who made the record of Wolverine Blues ever so flippin' with him? I don't recall. I can't remember that, about that time. Maybe that was Eddie Miller's number, but I still think some others. No, it doesn't ring the bell with me. No, there were some others too. Where he plays clarinet, I don't know. Some of the Mound City Blue Blowers, which were really kind of- I believe this was Bob Crosby.
The big band? The big band. The big band.
It could be South Rumpal Street Parade or something like that. I can't recall a fan. But what about guys like Perini? Who was he playing with to get along? He was starving to death at the time.

Plenty of us were. That was not unusual at all. There was a little guitar player from this town who's still here now by the name of Clayton Dyrd, I think it's D-U-E-R-R-R, D-E-U-R-R, known as Sunshine. A very fine guitar player. He played with the Joe Venuti Trio a while. And George Hartman from here. There were a whole bunch of people. I don't know how an upstate New York guy who was living and rooming with all these New Orleans fellas, but that's the way it happened. None of us was any too affluent. It was a matter sometimes of grabbing a one-spot job a week if you could grab it. The depression was on in its depths and money was scarce. Yet if you did grab a job or two, it would see you through just one or two spots. They called them club dates then. They didn't call them spot jobs. That's a New Orleans term I guess. They were strictly called club dates in New York. You get a club date. But of course they were all there hanging around waiting for the big chance, the chance to join up with a big road band or to make it big. A little band, Louis Prima, who must have been pretty young then, if I believe the age I saw a club printed for him recently in a magazine. Had a band in the old famous store, the first famous store. And he had, if I recall, practically Joe Marcella playing clarinet with him. And then later Joe Marcella moved over to the Hickory House with Winnie Anone playing clarinet. And there was a really fine clarinet player, Joe Marcella. Very good. Wasn't he originally from Buffalo, New York? No, I think he was from Chicago.
No, Chicago.
That's right. And there was another one from Buffalo, I think of it, named Hank DiMico, who also played around in quite a few bands and was rated very well. He was the Buffalo boy, Hank DiMico.
I don't know what's happened to him then.
Nor I.
Marcella doesn't play anymore, no?
Doesn't play anymore at all, I imagine.
I don't think so. He composed, maybe composes now. He had one hit, don't you remember? Don't cry at Joe? Oh yes, I remember.
I never connected that with Joe, my solid clarinet player.
That was him.

I played with his brother Marty Marcella. So I played once in a band that was gotten together and managed by Ben Pollack, but it was under the name of Cheeple Marks, the first brothers. And in that band Marty Marcella was playing. George Wettling played drums in it. Quite a few other guys like that.
Back to Clayton Dorr, who was he playing with? Just spots? He didn't?

Oh, he played with some of the bands. Some of these bands that had a semi-name in those days are completely forgotten today. It was a band named Bob Sylvester that he played with. And when I met him, he was living with Bob Sylvester because he never had collected any money from him. And the only way he could collect any money from him was to live with him and deduct the lodging from what Sylvester owed him. And that was typical of the business in those days. And I guess the best he ever did was playing the stint with Joe Vanuti. Because Joe always had a name.
What about George Horton? Was he playing trumpet there? He played trumpet.

He also played bass, but primarily trumpet. And in fact he played some darn good trumpet as I remember. Some really good New Orleans trumpet. But it was a hard thing to get into. Johnny Beresdorf was up there playing good trumpet too. But one thing I noticed about most of the New Orleans guys, with very few exceptions, they were pining for New Orleans all the time. Longing to get back and it didn't take much to convince them that they belonged back to New Orleans. That's a trait peculiar to the city. The people that are born here seem to find it very hard to live happily anywhere else.
Well, there's something unique about the town. It's got to be.
Whether it's the coffee or the Mardi Gras or something.
Well, Pete Fountain, when they gave this Welcome Back Pete concert over at Macalice, he said it was French bread that he longed all night in.
Yeah.
And others talking about red beans and rye. Right. But I know you worked some dates with Bill Bourgeois.

Yes, I did with George Hartman too. We'd pick up spot jobs here and there. In fact, when I came to this town after all those many years, Bill Bourgeois reminded me that we had played together for a Jewish leader up in New York at a dance celebrating Hitler's birthday. His memory was better than mine though. I'd forgotten it until he mentioned it. And you know, you had a clique and you tried to help each other out with spot jobs. So we'd actually moved around somewhat and meet them off and together on jobs.
How big a band was that playing for the district? Probably eight men.
That was quite usual. But I don't remember. There were a lot of halls there that had eight-piece minimums in New York. Who's the leader? Lou Lockman. Lou Lockett. Lou Lockett.
That's it, Lou Lockett.

Bill can check that for you. He knows for sure. He knows the name. He's the leader. But with an eight-piece band you could sort of imitate swing a little I guess. Oh, I used to play a lot of jazz. You could choruses all the time, sure. But I mean you could get some, that was a flexible band.
Yeah, but usually you see they played stocks because these bands weren't in any way organized.

As a matter of fact, it was quite customary in New York for a guy to book all the jobs he could. He never turned a job down. He might, if he were really hot or had lucky, he might book say three jobs on a Saturday night. And the reason he booked those jobs was so that he could give two of them to friends of
his.

And so it was nothing for a leader to go in the union hall and hire a band, you know, engage the different musicians. And then when he got on the job he was apt to find that half of them or even more were guys he hadn't seen before. You see, you'd come in and sort of say, Benny sent me here, Joe sent me. And this was alright so long as you cut the job. You didn't jeopardize the connection of the guy that had booked it. This was common practice.
So long as you could read stocks. Read stocks was about all that.

Oh yeah, read the stocks and occasionally the guy might have a few little sheets he'd scratched out and read those and play some jazz if that's what you were supposed to do. We're coming to the end of the tape.

I thought I'd get off on a long ramping subject. And it came to me. We talked one time about what style it was, you know, like a man could be reading music, say reading lead saxophone part and give an entirely different sound of the section. Absolutely.

But you can see that today in say a band like Les Elgart. It's true that they have distinctive music in the arrangement but there is also a distinctive sound to the sax section as they follow the leader. A very distinctive sound, different from any other band. But there was much more of that in those days. For every band the section would have a distinctive sound. Sometimes in the brass it was harder to do this in the brass but Isham Jones' brass had a distinctive sound to it. And very often the sax because there was so much leeway all the way from a lombardo style to a much more solid style and then the style that Goodman introduced when he had the first Mandela and then Jaime Schertzer playing lead sax. Very distinctive sounds. But earlier, this is what make a band. A lot of bands had nothing but stocks. But they all sound quite different. They cut up stocks a little bit. They make their own cuts and sort of maybe put the ending up for an introduction and things like that to make their band sound a little different. But the main difference came from the fact that the way they play these things. They took quite a lot of liberties. Not just with the sound but sometimes they even took liberties with the actual way the music was written and the side men, the section men, just had to follow the leader. They got used to the way they played. This made it very hard to bring a strange man in the band, you see.
But what do you think it is that makes for a style?
Well, I think…
I'm talking about either in section work or solo or what have you.

Well, partly of course, insofar as the style depended on tone, even his mouth formation would have something to do with that and perhaps the way he learned to blow, the kind of strength he had and the tone he produced. But then, a feeling, you get into the intangibles again and that feeling might be in part something innate but also in part the whole environment that he grew up in. The men he listened to, the men he worked with, the thing that soaked into him most to give him his approach. And then of course, the last and ultimate thing, I guess no guy ever really gets quite what he's looking for. He has a kind of ideal and he strives very hard to play that way but most all people fall short of their ideal. I've seen many musicians slam the horn down, throw it against the wall, not just because they missed a note but because generally they weren't getting what they were trying to get as a harp. And they'll mess around with mouthpieces and new horns and everything else. And if they're happy and successful, they're always coming closer to that ideal way of
playing. Well, to get down to a specific personal case, do you try to play one style yourself or do you vary your style a lot depending on who you're playing with?

Because I've played so long, I don't even try to vary my style. I'm forced to vary my style. I've tried to keep up all these years and if I'm playing with a modern group, I play modern. But if I'm playing with a Dixie group, say, a traditional group, I play as best I can. It certainly has that kind of overall feeling, traditional.
